Le Black Healing Centre : un havre de gu: The Black Healing Centre: A Black Haven of Healing Takes Root in Montréal
Le Black Healing Centre est un espace à: The Black Healing Centre is a space in Montréal that redefines well-being through intersectional, Afrocentric and community-based approaches.
Samantha Nyinawumuntu, fondatrice du Bla: Samantha Nyinawumuntu, founder of the Black Healing Centre, embodies the vision behind this community project. Photo credit: Nantou Soumahoro
J’ai voulu écrire cet article parce que: I wanted to write this article because, too often, when we talk about mental health, we act as if everyone starts from the same place, with the same needs and the same reference points.
À Montréal, trouver des espaces dédiés à: In Montréal, it is rare to find spaces devoted to the mental health and well-being of Black communities. And as I dug around online, one name kept coming up: the Black Healing Centre.
Un centre qui parle de guérison pour les: A centre that talks about healing for Black people, with an approach that takes into account who they are, what they have lived and their history, and that is not easy to find. Among other things, they offer collective care circles, retreats, and conversations about intergenerational trauma... This isn’t just one more form of therapy, it’s another way of thinking about care. An unconventional approach, rooted in the community.
Ça m’a poussée à me poser des questions: It made me start asking questions: Who are they? How was this centre created? What does a space where healing is collective, not individual, actually look like? What does it mean to heal “together”?
En creusant ces questions, j’ai découver: As I explored these questions, I discovered a place that is reinventing care and healing for Black communities in Montréal. A space where people gather, share and rebuild together, far from conventional models and closer to lived experience and collective resilience.
<strong>Cela fait déjà cinq ans que le B: The Black Healing Centre, a non-profit organization designed by and for Black communities, has existed for five years now. Until recently, it had no physical space of its own to welcome its members for activities. Since the end of April 2025, the Black Healing Centre finally has a space, on the border between the Côte-des-Neiges and Notre-Dame-de-Grâce neighbourhoods in Montréal. With a permanent range of services such as collective care circles, and one-off activities such as candlelit yin yoga sessions, “open mic” nights for queer and trans Black people, or writing and mindfulness workshops, the space has become a community hub where care dedicated to Black people abounds. A look back at what this place means to some of its members, and at its inauguration night last April.
C’était un soir pluvieux à la fin du moi: It was a rainy evening at the end of April 2025. The Queen Mary health complex, at 2100 Marlowe Avenue, seems deserted. Almost every office is dark, except one, on the 4th floor: the Black Healing Centre.
Le choix de s’installer à proximité du m: The choice to settle near Vendôme metro station is no accident. It is located where the community lives and reflects a clear intention: to make services accessible and anchored in the daily lives of the people concerned. Too often, community spaces are far away and hard to reach.
Pour l’atteindre, il a fallu d’abord s’e: To get there, you first have to make your way through the building’s silent maze: corridors with dull walls, discreet elevators, hidden stairwells. A route like a well-kept secret, leading to suite 449, where the inauguration night was held.
À l’intérieur, le contraste est saisissa:
Inside, the contrast is striking. About fifty people embrace, exchange knowing glances and hearty laughter. A collective sense of pride is palpable. Because this place was something they wanted, but it almost never existed. Too expensive. Too Black. Too community-oriented.

“We lost a lot of money. We had to deal with a lot of white people telling us: ‘No, you can’t come here,’” says the centre’s board chair, Danièle-Jocelyne Otou, opening her speech.
« Il y a à peine six mois, Dieu sait que: “Barely six months ago, God knows we were about to pull the plug. But we didn’t, and I am so happy we didn’t. We deserve a space that allows us to take care of ourselves,” she continues.
Si des portes se sont fermées les unes a: Although doors closed one after another, the space is now very much here. The centre’s clinical director and psychotherapist, Dr. Lisa Ndejuru, celebrates this in her remarks.
« L'espace, ce n’est pas [juste] les mur: “The space is not [just] the walls. It’s the people. It’s the dream taking shape.” Lisa Ndejuru gives the people who came to celebrate the centre’s official opening a kind of voice for the collective journey through the tunnel that they endured to reach this inauguration. In the room, the moment is solemn, and silence reigns.
« Ce travail a commencé avant que le mon: “This work began before the world was set ablaze, before George Floyd lost his breath [...] We did not look away. We stayed. We stood shoulder to shoulder. We cried. We worked. We sowed. We harvested hope from the soil. The world is still struggling. It has not stopped. But we, we keep the fire burning.” Her words are punctuated by a few “amens” from the audience.
Derrière les murs du Black Healing Centr: Behind the walls of the Black Healing Centre lies the personal story of its founder, Samantha Nyinawumuntula. That of a long search for a safe space where she could feel understood. The first therapist she met was not Black: “I remember finishing the session and thinking, ‘I don’t think this is for me,’” she says in her soft, measured voice.
Durant la pandémie, le manque d’espace c: During the pandemic, the lack of dedicated space became even more glaring. “Everyone was on a one-year waiting list for a CLSC (local community service centre) or to find a therapist. And when you add Black therapists, they were all overwhelmed and exhausted too.”
Samantha passe donc à l’action. C’est en: So Samantha took action. In 2020, the idea of creating a space designed by and for Black people took root, just as the effects of isolation and stress were being felt acutely. She then sounded out the community. The question she asked was simple: “A centre dedicated to our well-being, is that something you want?” The answer was unanimous. “Everyone said yes, a centre dedicated to the well-being of Black people is something we want,” says Samantha.
En 2021, de premières offres de services: In 2021, the first services were launched. Over the years, the permanent offering took shape: collective care, a training program for community care practitioners, retreats. At the Black Healing Centre, mental health is approached differently, by reconnecting body, history and identity, within a space that is openly and deliberately for Black people only. How? By offering Afrocentric, community-based and intersectional approaches.
Princella (left) and Patricia (right). It was about time to have a space where Black people can gather to talk about, among other things, mental health. Photo credit: Nantou Soumahoro
Popularisé par la chercheuse afro-améric: Popularized by African-American scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw, the concept of intersectionality helps us understand how different forms of oppression, including racism, sexism, homophobia and transphobia, intersect and amplify one another. For Samantha Niyinawumuntu, it is impossible to talk about mental health without taking this dimension into account: “Well-being also means thinking about intersectionality: Black people are not all the same.”
Cette approche se traduit concrètement p: In practice, this approach takes the form of collective care circles inspired by Afro-Caribbean traditions, designed for women, men, and queer and trans people. Each circle runs for 12 weeks and often ends with a retreat in nature. The groups are led by facilitators who share lived experiences similar to those of the participants, because the paths to healing cannot be universal.
Pour les hommes, la question de la santé: For men, the subject of mental health often remains more taboo and meets with more reluctance. When the program for women was launched, many men came forward asking: “What about us?” But creating a space for discussion suited to them meant finding other ways in. They said they did not want to hear about “healing” explicitly, preferring to include more activities and use different vocabulary. That is how the idea came about of organizing, for example, wellness days in barbershops, places where men naturally feel more at ease. Their openness to well-being is real, but it is essential to involve them from the design stage of programs in order to meet their specific needs.
La guérison passe aussi par la reconnais: Healing also involves recognizing wounds passed down from generation to generation. For Samantha, systemic racism and the legacies of colonialism have left deep wounds that continue to affect Black communities today. “I believe we need to build community ties and have more of these conversations. Not by trivializing them, but by offering more spaces where we can talk about what we live through within our community. It will help people begin to understand what intergenerational trauma really is, because it’s still a very new concept for many communities to grasp.”
Et elle enchaîne : « Ce n’est pas juste: And she goes on: “It’s not just what your parents passed down to you, it’s also what you experienced at school, at work, and in other systems.”
<strong>« Nous sommes, pour la plupart,: “For the most part, we are one of the first generations to undertake this work. These are things we’ve been carrying for 400, 500 years [...] This legacy continues to affect how we are and how we react.”
La guérison collective est un processus: Collective healing is a long process that takes time and patience, Samantha emphasizes. According to her, it all starts with a personal commitment: becoming aware of what you are going through, identifying your needs, then looking for where to find suitable support and care. To make access easier, most of the services offered by the Black Healing Centre are free or low-cost, allowing more people to benefit from accessible support.
Une murale collective a été réalisée lor: A collective mural was created during the inauguration night, under the supervision of artist Kezna Dalz. Young and old took part. Photo credit: Nantou Soumahoro
Manda, aussi connue sous le nom de Miss: Manda, also known as Miss Benn on the airwaves of community radio station CKUT, has been coming to the centre since its early days. Born in Quebec, she grew up in a Caribbean culture marked by silence on the subject. “My parents didn’t talk about mental health. You lived, period.”
Ce mutisme l’a suivie jusqu’à l’âge adul: That silence followed her into adulthood, even into the institutions meant to support her. Manda looks back on her experience with conventional mental health services, notably those of the CLSC, which she used but found ineffective and disconnected from her reality. She gives an example: “They don’t understand our history. You don’t even live in my neighbourhood. So you don’t understand what we’re going through when we talk about abusive landlords.” For her, conventional psychological help may be well-intentioned, but it often fails because it does not take into account the specific cultural and social realities of the people it is trying to support. This gap shaped her conviction that the conventional mental health care system “wasn’t for her.”
Le Black Healing Centre a donc représent: The Black Healing Centre therefore represented a breath of fresh air and a space where she could finally feel recognized in her identity and her struggles. She then decided to “go back to the root of her traumas” and discovered the collective care circles for Black women.
« Il n’y a pas de mots pour les explique: “There are no words to explain them,” she says. She remembers the first sessions, when silence reigned, punctuated by tears. The simple act of crying together in a safe space became an act of liberation.
Un jour, un exercice bouleverse Manda. O: One day, an exercise shook Manda. She was asked to feel her body, from head to toe. She couldn’t. The facilitator insisted, gently digging deeper. And suddenly, a truth surfaced: Manda realized she had never grieved her mother, who died about ten years earlier. “I didn’t know I had mommy issues. We talk a lot about daddy issues, but we forget our mothers.”
Ce travail, dit-elle, lui a permis de co: This work, she says, helped her understand that some of the weight she carried did not belong to her, that it was inherited from collective pain that had to be untangled in order to move forward. “The things we carry are heavy. We have bricks in our bag and it’s simply a matter of unloading them.”
Au Black Healing Centre, elle dit avoir: At the Black Healing Centre, she says she found a new strength, a path toward mental and spiritual healing, through collective recognition and sisterhood. “I learned to breathe. Literally.”
Manda suit actuellement une formation av: Manda is currently in training with the Black Healing Centre to become an ancestral healing practitioner. The training allows her to deepen her knowledge and skills so that she can, in turn, support others on their healing journeys, drawing on cultural and community-based approaches suited to the reality of Black people.
Elle sait que la guérison n’est pas magi: She knows that healing isn’t magic, and that everyone moves at their own pace.
« Je ne dirais pas que le Black Healing: “I wouldn’t say the Black Healing Centre is going to ‘save you,’ because that creates expectations. But I can guarantee you’ll find refuge there. And sometimes, that’s all we need to get started,” she concludes.
Durant la soirée d’inauguration, chaque: During the inauguration night, every gesture, every word seemed to say: “We’re here. Finally.”
Pour Sayid, père de famille venu accompa: For Sayid, a father who came with his daughter, creating a physical space like the Black Healing Centre was “crucial.” Walking through the centre’s doors, he says he felt a deep sense of belonging: “When you see people like you, who are dealing with similar problems, with whom you can share your stories, your hopes, your successes, it’s incredible,” he says.
Sayid se réjouit de pouvoir enfin compte: Sayid is delighted to finally be able to count on a place like the Black Healing Centre. Photo credit: Nantou Soumahoro
Sur le point de quitter l'événement, deu: Just as they were about to leave the event, two other participants, Patricia and Princella, head out with radiant faces. “I think it’s important to have a space that’s representative of the Black population. A lot of trauma has been handed down through all kinds of histories. And I think we’ve needed to start shedding this trauma for a long time,” Patricia explains.
Il est temps pour les membres de la comm: It’s time for members of the Black community to go to therapy and to say so loud and clear, she argues. “We’re really seeing a kind of democratization of mental health in the Black community, among women, men and children alike. I think it’s important to claim it and normalize it.”
Dans la salle commune du Black Healing C: In the Black Healing Centre’s common room, a collective painting imagined by artist Kezna Dalz, made of flowers and faces and bearing the message “Intentionally Healing,” leaves a living imprint of the evening, recalling the presence and commitment of everyone who wants to be part of this paradigm shift.
